description: We are a team of high school students who came together to participate in an international hackathon, gain experience, and explore new opportunities. We are interested in science, physics, programming, technology, and personal development. Our skills include coding, physics, research, problem-solving, creativity, and English communication. We value teamwork, sharing ideas, learning from each other, and challenging ourselves through new experiences.
summary:
AeroMargin is a website that helps astronauts plan safe walks on Mars. Most Mars maps show what the ground looks like, but they don't tell you how much oxygen it takes to cross it. We built a map that does.
You pick a start point and a target, and AeroMargin finds the safest route instead of the shortest one. The map is split into safe, caution and restricted zones. An oxygen calculator estimates how much air the trip will use, based on slope, soil type, fatigue, suit mass and Mars gravity. details:
AeroMargin is a web app for planning safe walks on the surface of Mars. The user picks a starting point, usually the habitat airlock, and a target such as a science site. The app finds the safest route between them. The safest path is often not the shortest one, because loose sand and steep slopes cost much more energy and oxygen than flat, firm ground.
The map is split into safe, caution and restricted zones. As a route is built, an oxygen calculator estimates how much air the trip will use. The model takes into account slope, soil type, astronaut fatigue, a suit mass of 195 kg and Mars gravity of 3.721 m/s². Routes are chosen with Dijkstra's algorithm, where each step costs its oxygen use plus a safety penalty. A point-of-no-return boundary shows how far the astronaut can go and still have enough oxygen to get back to the airlock. Crew members can mark hazards they find, with a type, risk level and description, and the planner then routes around them. Voice control and photos support these core functions.
The main benefit is that astronauts can make safe decisions on their own. A message to Earth takes 4 to 24 minutes each way, so in an emergency there's no time to wait for mission control. Before leaving, the crew can see whether a trip is safe and whether they'll have the oxygen to return. Mission planners also get the oxygen cost of each route, which helps them choose which science targets are worth the trip. We hope tools like this make longer and more ambitious surface missions possible without adding risk to the crew.
We built AeroMargin as a website using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages, with the code managed on GitHub. We made the demo slides in Canva. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write and debug code and to translate our materials into English.
What makes the project creative is its focus. Most Mars maps answer the question "what does the ground look like?" Ours answers "will I make it back?" Showing oxygen as a map layer, with a moving return boundary, turns a resource number into something an astronaut can understand at a glance.
We tried to be honest about what the prototype can and can't do. The demo terrain is synthetic, modeled on Melas Chasma in Valles Marineris, and the oxygen model still needs calibration, so every number is an estimate. We kept real orbital data, Gale Crater calibration data and synthetic demo data clearly separate. Next we plan to add NASA's MOLA and CTX data and ESA's HRSC data, validate the oxygen model, add shared hazard reports, and test an AR version for a helmet display or AR glasses.
